ed-monitoring-l01.q: Which parameter's number can be used as a mechanical cross-check against an ECG-derived heart rate that might be counting artifact?
choices: Respiratory rate
The pulse rate from the SpO2 pleth waveform
NIBP mean pressure
Temperature
ed-monitoring-l01.why: The SpO2 sensor reads an actual pulsatile flow at the finger, an independent mechanical signal, so it can confirm or contradict the ECG-derived rate. The others don't measure heart rate at all.

ed-monitoring-l01.q: The chart shows NIBP 118/76 from 12 minutes ago. The patient now looks pale and diaphoretic. What should you do?
choices: Trust the charted number since 12 minutes is recent
Wait for the next scheduled automatic cycle
Manually cycle the cuff now and reassess
Assume the SpO2 will catch the change first
ed-monitoring-l01.why: NIBP is a snapshot, not continuous. A changed clinical picture invalidates an old number; recheck it by hand immediately rather than waiting or trusting a stale value.

ed-monitoring-l02.q: A patient's heart rate is 132 from pain, above the default high-rate alarm limit. What is the correct response?
choices: Silence the alarm permanently
Treat the underlying pain and let the alarm reflect the real, abnormal rate
Raise the high-rate limit so it stops alarming
Turn the alarm volume down
ed-monitoring-l02.why: The alarm is accurate here — the rate really is elevated. Widening the limit or silencing hides a true abnormal finding instead of addressing its cause.

ed-monitoring-l02.q: Which of these is a legitimate reason to widen an alarm limit for a specific patient?
choices: The alarm is annoying nearby staff
A documented baseline, such as chronic rate-controlled atrial fibrillation in the 90s, makes the default limit wrong for this patient
The same alarm has fired twice in ten minutes
The patient is currently asleep
ed-monitoring-l02.why: Limits are adjusted only for a patient's real, documented physiology, per protocol — never for staff convenience or alarm frequency alone.

ed-monitoring-l03.q: A patient scheduled for a pulse ox reading has dark nail polish on the only accessible finger. What should you do?
choices: Place the probe there and treat the reading as reliable
Recognize the reading may be falsely low or unreadable, and use an unpolished finger or the ear instead
Increase supplemental oxygen to compensate
Place two probes on adjacent fingers and average the readings
ed-monitoring-l03.why: Dark polish absorbs light and can block or distort the sensor's signal. The fix is a different site, not compensating with oxygen or trusting a corrupted number.

ed-monitoring-l03.q: A patient with a crush injury to the arm carrying the pulse ox probe shows SpO2 92% with a weak, irregular pleth. What do you check first?
choices: Move the probe to an uninjured extremity or the ear and confirm the waveform is clean there
Chart 92% as an accurate value
Apply a blood pressure cuff on that same arm to boost the signal
Assume carbon monoxide poisoning
ed-monitoring-l03.why: Local perfusion loss from the injury is corrupting the reading at that site. Moving to a site with normal perfusion and a clean waveform is the fix before trusting or acting on the number.

ed-monitoring-l04.q: During transport a capnography sampling line kinks. EtCO2 reads 0 with no waveform, but the patient is breathing comfortably and SpO2 is 99%. What is the likely cause?
choices: Esophageal intubation
Cardiac arrest
A mechanical obstruction of the sampling line, not a physiologic problem
Massive pulmonary embolism
ed-monitoring-l04.why: A flat trace with a well-appearing, well-saturating patient points to a mechanical circuit problem — most often a kinked or obstructed line — rather than a true physiologic event.

ed-monitoring-l04.q: A sedated patient on nasal cannula oxygen has EtCO2 climbing from 40 to 58 mmHg while SpO2 stays 98%. What does this show before SpO2 changes at all?
choices: Nothing concerning, since SpO2 is normal
Early hypoventilation — EtCO2 rises well before supplemental oxygen lets SpO2 fall
A capnography sensor malfunction
Metabolic alkalosis
ed-monitoring-l04.why: Supplemental oxygen masks a falling SpO2 for minutes after breathing slows, but exhaled CO2 rises immediately, which is exactly why capnography catches hypoventilation earlier than pulse ox in this setting.

ed-monitoring-l05.q: An 80 kg adult needs a blood pressure and only a pediatric-sized (too small) cuff is available. What artifact should you expect?
choices: A falsely low reading
A falsely high reading
No meaningful effect
The cuff will fail to inflate
ed-monitoring-l05.why: A cuff bladder that is too narrow for the arm overestimates pressure, producing a falsely high reading — the opposite error from an oversized cuff.

ed-monitoring-l05.q: A patient has a dialysis fistula in the left arm and no other access issues. Where should the blood pressure cuff go?
choices: The left arm, since it is closest
The right arm, or a thigh if needed — never over a fistula or graft
Either arm briefly is acceptable
The ankle only, regardless of arm status
ed-monitoring-l05.why: Cuff pressure on a fistula or graft arm can damage it or occlude flow. The unaffected arm, or a properly sized thigh cuff, is used instead, and the choice is documented.

ed-monitoring-l06.q: A patient's heart rate is 128 and systolic blood pressure is 118. Calculate the shock index and interpret it.
choices: About 1.1 — elevated, suggesting possible compensated shock even though each number looks acceptable alone
About 0.9 — normal
About 1.1 — a normal finding in a patient who is simply anxious
It cannot be calculated without a respiratory rate
ed-monitoring-l06.why: 128 divided by 118 is roughly 1.1, above the 0.9 threshold that flags serious illness even when heart rate and blood pressure individually look reassuring.

ed-monitoring-l06.q: Which combination best signals early organ hypoperfusion even while every number stays inside the alarm limits?
choices: Warm, dry skin with brisk capillary refill
Capillary refill over 3 seconds, mottled skin, and urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h
A single normal blood pressure reading
A patient who requests a blanket
ed-monitoring-l06.why: Cap refill, skin findings, and urine output are direct, hands-on signs of organ perfusion that change before alarm limits are breached — exactly the kind of finding a monitor alone will miss.

ed-monitoring-l07.q: A patient has a temperature of 38.6C, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 24, and white blood cell count 14,000. How many SIRS criteria are met?
ed-monitoring-l07.why: Temp over 38, HR over 90, RR over 20, and WBC over 12,000 are all met — all four SIRS criteria, well above the threshold of two used to flag concern.

ed-monitoring-l07.q: A patient is alert and oriented with a respiratory rate of 20 and a systolic blood pressure of 92. What is the qSOFA score?
ed-monitoring-l07.why: Only the systolic of 100 or less scores a point; respiratory rate must be 22 or more and mentation must be altered to score, neither of which applies here, giving qSOFA 1.

ed-monitoring-l08.q: Immediately after a shock is delivered during a code, what should happen next?
choices: A pulse check before anything else
Chest compressions resume immediately without a pulse check
The defibrillator is charged again right away
Epinephrine is given immediately
ed-monitoring-l08.why: Compressions resume the instant a shock is delivered — pausing to check a pulse wastes perfusion time on a rhythm that has not yet had a chance to organize.

ed-monitoring-l08.q: What compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in adult CPR without an advanced airway in place?
choices: Continuous compressions with a breath every 6 seconds
ed-monitoring-l08.why: 30 compressions to 2 breaths is standard for adult CPR until an advanced airway (such as an ET tube) is placed, after which compressions and ventilations become asynchronous.

ed-monitoring-l09.q: A restrained patient's distal circulation check is due. What must be assessed and documented?
choices: Only that the restraint knot is secure
Skin color, temperature, and pulses distal to the restraint, checked and documented on a regular interval
Blood pressure alone
Nothing until the provider rounds
ed-monitoring-l09.why: Restraints require ongoing distal circulation and skin checks on a set interval — the physical findings, not just knot security, are what catch a developing complication.

ed-monitoring-l09.q: A sedated ED patient is drowsy, opening her eyes only briefly to your voice — a RASS of -1. Is this within the usual ED target range?
choices: No, this requires immediate reversal
Yes, 0 to -2 is a typical ED target for a sedated patient
No, only a RASS of exactly 0 is acceptable
Yes, but only if the patient is intubated
ed-monitoring-l09.why: Most ED sedation targets fall between 0 and -2, so a -1 is within the expected range and does not by itself signal a problem.

ed-monitoring-l10.q: A low-SpO2 alarm fires while a patient is walking to the bathroom. The pleth is clean and reads 91%, and the patient says he feels fine. What is the first step?
choices: Silence it and move on since he feels fine
Look at the patient — assess work of breathing and mentation — before deciding what the number means
Turn off the SpO2 alarm for this patient without discussion
Assume motion artifact and disregard the number
ed-monitoring-l10.why: The algorithm starts with the patient, not the screen. A clean waveform with a low number and reported symptoms both need direct assessment before any conclusion is reached.

ed-monitoring-l10.q: Applying the three-question alarm algorithm in order, what comes first, second, and third?
choices: Silence, then look at the patient, then check the waveform
Does the waveform match the number, is there a fixable mechanical cause, and if not, escalate
Escalate immediately for every alarm regardless of cause
Check the waveform, escalate, then look at the patient
ed-monitoring-l10.why: After first looking at the patient, the sequence is: does the trace match the number, is there a mechanical fix available in thirty seconds, and if neither resolves it, escalate.

ed-monitoring-l11.q: Using the standard limb-lead color mnemonic, where does the white electrode go on a four- or five-lead system?
choices: Right arm or right upper chest
Left leg or left lower abdomen
Left upper chest
Center chest at V1
ed-monitoring-l11.why: "White on right" places the white electrode on the right arm or right upper chest, one anchor of the standard mnemonic used to place limb leads correctly.

ed-monitoring-l11.q: A monitored patient's displayed rate suddenly appears to double, and the extra beats line up exactly with visible pacemaker spikes. What is the likely explanation?
choices: A true doubling of the intrinsic heart rate
The monitor is counting each pacer spike as a separate beat along with the QRS complex
New ventricular fibrillation
Normal, accurate counting
ed-monitoring-l11.why: Pacer spikes, like tall T waves, can be miscounted as extra complexes, artificially doubling the displayed rate — the fix is checking against a palpated pulse and adjusting counting settings per policy.

ed-monitoring-l12.q: A capnogram's baseline never returns to zero between breaths, sitting elevated throughout. What does this generally indicate?
choices: Bronchospasm
Rebreathing of exhaled CO2, such as from inadequate fresh gas flow or a faulty valve
Esophageal intubation
A normal variant needing no action
ed-monitoring-l12.why: An elevated baseline that fails to reach zero between breaths is the classic sign of rebreathing exhaled gas, usually a circuit or valve problem rather than a patient problem.

ed-monitoring-l12.q: In a patient with falling cardiac output from shock but unchanged ventilation, what happens to EtCO2?
choices: It rises steadily
It falls, because less blood is reaching the lungs to carry CO2 for exhalation
It stays exactly the same
It becomes erratic with no discernible pattern
ed-monitoring-l12.why: EtCO2 depends on blood delivering CO2 to the lungs as well as on ventilation. When circulation drops while breathing continues unchanged, EtCO2 falls, reflecting the circulatory problem.

ed-monitoring-l13.q: A 100 kg septic patient needs the 30 mL/kg fluid bolus. How much fluid is needed, and how should it be delivered?
choices: 2000 mL through any working peripheral IV over 6 hours
3000 mL through large-bore access under a pressure bag or rapid infuser, not by gravity alone
1000 mL is the practical maximum regardless of weight
4500 mL through any peripheral line at a comfortable rate
ed-monitoring-l13.why: 30 mL/kg for a 100 kg patient is 3000 mL, and delivering that volume within the intended timeframe requires large-bore access and pressure-assisted infusion, not gravity alone.

ed-monitoring-l13.q: At the 1-3 hour sepsis reassessment, which single finding best confirms improving perfusion beyond a repeat blood pressure alone?
choices: A repeat temperature only
A falling lactate trend along with adequate urine output and improved perfusion signs
A normal white blood cell count
The patient's self-report of feeling better, taken alone
ed-monitoring-l13.why: Lactate clearance combined with urine output and hands-on perfusion findings gives an objective picture of whether treatment is working, more reliable than any single number or subjective report.

ed-monitoring-l14.q: A patient's GCS trends from E3 V4 M5 (12) to E2 V3 M4 (9) over one hour. What does this represent, and what should happen?
choices: Normal fluctuation that needs no action
A clinically significant decline that requires immediate reassessment and notification
An artifact of different examiners scoring differently, safe to ignore
An improvement, since fewer stimuli were needed to test him
ed-monitoring-l14.why: A 3-point drop in GCS, especially with worsening in more than one component, is a real and urgent decline that must be reported immediately, not attributed to scoring variability.

ed-monitoring-l14.q: Why is recording pupil size in millimeters, rather than describing it as 'normal' or 'large,' important?
choices: It is required for billing purposes
Precise measurement lets a new asymmetry or trend be objectively detected over time
Millimeters are simply faster to write
It has no real clinical value beyond habit
ed-monitoring-l14.why: A number lets subsequent exams be compared directly; a vague word like 'normal' cannot reveal a one- or two-millimeter change that may be the first sign of rising intracranial pressure.

ed-monitoring-l15.q: A patient's respiratory rate has been charted as 18 on the last three checks, though the tech has noted increasing work of breathing each time. What is the likely explanation and the risk?
choices: The rate genuinely has not changed
The rate is being estimated or copied forward instead of counted, masking real deterioration
This confirms the patient is stable
Monitors count respiratory rate perfectly, so there is no risk here
ed-monitoring-l15.why: An uncounted, copied-forward rate can hide a genuine trend. Respiratory rate must be actually counted, especially when other findings like increased work of breathing suggest it should be changing.

ed-monitoring-l15.q: Which patient is showing deterioration disguised as improvement?
choices: A febrile patient whose temperature normalizes after antipyretics and antibiotics
An anxious, wheezing asthmatic who suddenly becomes calm and quiet with a silent chest
A patient whose heart rate falls from 140 to 90 after adequate pain control
A dehydrated patient whose heart rate falls after a fluid bolus
ed-monitoring-l15.why: A silent chest in an asthmatic who was previously wheezing loudly means too little air is moving to make a wheeze — impending respiratory failure, not calm improvement. The other options reflect genuine, expected improvement.

ed-monitoring-l16.q: Using the '70 plus twice the age in years' rule, what is the estimated lower limit of normal systolic blood pressure for an 8-year-old?
choices: 70 mmHg
78 mmHg
86 mmHg
90 mmHg
ed-monitoring-l16.why: 70 plus (2 times 8) equals 86 mmHg, the estimated lower limit of normal systolic pressure for a child of that age.

ed-monitoring-l16.q: An infant is tachycardic and tachypneic but has a normal blood pressure. How should this be interpreted?
choices: The infant is stable since the blood pressure is normal
Children compensate well and can maintain a normal blood pressure until very late, so tachycardia and tachypnea alone are taken seriously
Blood pressure is the earliest and most reliable indicator of illness in children
No action is needed until the blood pressure actually drops
ed-monitoring-l16.why: Pediatric patients compensate effectively, so a normal blood pressure can persist even as a child deteriorates. Tachycardia and tachypnea are earlier, more reliable warning signs and should not be dismissed because the blood pressure still looks normal.

ed-monitoring-l17.q: A patient in recovery after procedural sedation is fully awake, moves all four limbs on command, has a blood pressure within 20 mmHg of baseline, breathes deeply and coughs freely, and maintains 94% on room air. What is her Aldrete score out of 10?
choices: It cannot be scored without a formal RASS assessment
ed-monitoring-l17.why: Each of the five Aldrete categories — activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, and saturation — scores 2 points when fully met, and every criterion here is fully met, giving a total of 10.

ed-monitoring-l17.q: Five minutes after a sedation procedure ends, why is this considered the highest-risk window for the patient?
choices: Because monitoring is typically stopped at that point
Because peak drug effect can arrive once the painful stimulus that was keeping the patient aroused stops
Because the patient is usually discharged at that exact moment
Because vitals are not checked during this window
ed-monitoring-l17.why: Procedural pain can mask a drug's full effect while it is happening. Once the stimulus ends, sedation can deepen suddenly, which is why monitoring continues closely through this window rather than easing up.

ed-monitoring-l18.q: Which of these is a 'softening phrase' that should be avoided in a rapid response call?
choices: "I need someone at the bedside now"
"Whenever you get a chance..."
"Respiratory rate rose from 18 to 28 in 40 minutes"
"Systolic dropped from 128 to 88"
ed-monitoring-l18.why: Phrases like "whenever you get a chance" turn an urgent request into something that can be queued and delayed. Numbers and a direct, specific ask are what actually move a clinician to the bedside.

ed-monitoring-l18.q: What must accompany a monitored patient during any transport off the unit, such as to radiology?
choices: Nothing extra if the trip is expected to be short
A named escort, a charged transport monitor, and enough oxygen and airway equipment for the round trip
Just the wheelchair or stretcher
A note left for the receiving department to read later
ed-monitoring-l18.why: A monitored patient needs continuous monitoring and airway readiness throughout transport, not just at the destination — an escort, working equipment, and adequate oxygen for the whole trip are required.

quiz.q: A monitor's ECG-derived heart rate reads 140, but the patient's radial pulse counted by hand is 70. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The monitor is double-counting a tall T wave or similar artifact as an extra beat per cycle
The radial pulse is unreliable and should be disregarded
The patient has a true rate of 140 with a weak pulse
The ECG cable needs to be replaced regardless of the rate
quiz.why: A doubled displayed rate with a much lower palpated pulse is the classic pattern of electrical double-counting, not a true tachycardia. Confirming by hand is exactly how this is caught.

quiz.q: Which statement about the monitor's derived respiratory rate is accurate?
choices: It directly measures airflow through the nose and mouth
It is calculated from chest impedance changes between ECG electrodes, so talking and movement can be miscounted as breaths
It is always more accurate than a manually counted rate
It cannot be displayed unless capnography is attached
quiz.why: Impedance pneumography infers breathing from small changes in electrical resistance between chest electrodes, which movement and talking can mimic, producing a falsely high or erratic number.

quiz.q: A tech is orienting a new hire and explains why monitor colors cannot be trusted blindly. What is the best reason given?
choices: All monitors use identical colors by federal regulation
Color only matters for the ECG waveform
Color conventions vary by manufacturer and can be reconfigured, so the actual unit's screen must be learned directly
Colors change automatically based on patient acuity
quiz.why: There is a common convention, but it is not universal or fixed — vendors and departments vary it, so relying on a memorized color rule instead of the actual screen in front of you is a trap.

quiz.q: A tech silences a repeatedly firing SpO2 alarm from the central nursing station without walking to the room. What is wrong with this action?
choices: Nothing, silencing from the station saves time
It is fine as long as it is documented afterward
It is only a problem if the patient is unstable
Silencing should only happen at the bedside, after seeing the patient and identifying the cause
quiz.why: Silencing an alarm without seeing the patient is making a clinical judgment about someone you have not assessed. The rule is bedside first, silence second.

quiz.q: A pediatric patient's heart rate of 130 is well above the adult default high-rate alarm limit. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: This is likely a normal rate for a young child, and the limit should be adjusted to the correct pediatric range rather than silenced repeatedly
The child is in a dangerous tachycardia regardless of age
The alarm should be permanently disabled for pediatric patients
Default adult limits are always appropriate for children
quiz.why: Default limits are calibrated for adults and are wrong for children by design. The fix is setting age-appropriate limits for this patient, not ignoring or disabling the alarm.

quiz.q: Over a busy shift, a tech notices staff responding more slowly to alarms as the day goes on. What underlying process explains this, and why does it matter?
choices: Staff fatigue from walking; it only affects efficiency
Alarm fatigue from a high rate of false or insignificant alarms, which trains staff to ignore alarms and delays response to real events
The monitors are malfunctioning as the day progresses
It reflects appropriate prioritization and is not a concern
quiz.why: Alarm fatigue is a well-documented patient safety hazard: constant false alarms desensitize staff, so a genuinely dangerous alarm can be missed or delayed among the noise.

quiz.q: A patient in a cold ambulance bay has an SpO2 reading of 88% with a small, ragged pleth waveform, but is speaking full sentences with no distress. What is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Immediately apply high-flow oxygen and prepare for intubation
Chart the value and continue without further action
Warm the extremity, try another site, and look for a clean waveform before trusting the number
Assume the equipment is broken and replace the entire monitor
quiz.why: Cold, poorly perfused extremities are a classic cause of a falsely low reading with a poor waveform. The clinical picture (comfortable, speaking in full sentences) doesn't match a true SpO2 of 88, so the site is checked before treating the number as real.

quiz.q: Which patient's pulse oximetry reading is least trustworthy as written, without further context?
choices: A calm, resting patient with a clean pleth waveform reading 98%
A patient sleeping quietly with a regular pleth reading 96%
A resting patient with an appropriately sized probe reading 97%
A patient found in a house fire, altered and headachy, reading 99% on room air
quiz.why: Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin, so a smoke-exposed, altered patient with a normal-looking reading may actually have carbon monoxide poisoning — the number is falsely reassuring.

quiz.q: A patient's SpO2 reads 100% with a perfectly clean waveform, but the patient is agitated, confused, and was found near a running generator in a closed garage. What should you consider before trusting the 100%?
choices: Carbon monoxide exposure, since standard oximetry cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and will read falsely high or normal
The reading is definitely accurate since the waveform is clean
A probe placement error is the only likely explanation
The patient's confusion is unrelated to the exposure
quiz.why: A clean waveform confirms the sensor is reading well, but it cannot fix the fundamental limitation that standard pulse oximetry cannot detect carbon monoxide — clinical suspicion from the history has to override a reassuring number.

quiz.q: A patient is receiving bag-valve-mask ventilation after a witnessed collapse. The capnography waveform shows no trace at all despite visible chest rise. What is the most urgent concern to rule out first?
choices: A calibration error that can wait until after the code
A dislodged or misplaced airway, or esophageal placement, since a flat trace with attempted ventilation is a critical finding
Normal variation that requires no action
The sensor simply needs to warm up for several minutes
quiz.why: A completely flat capnogram during active ventilation efforts is treated as airway misplacement or disconnection until proven otherwise, because this is the highest-stakes explanation and the one that kills quickly if missed.

quiz.q: During ongoing CPR, EtCO2 rises from 12 to 38 mmHg and stays there for over a minute without any change in compression technique. What should the team suspect?
choices: A capnography malfunction requiring immediate replacement
Worsening acidosis
Possible return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), prompting a pulse check
Nothing significant; EtCO2 fluctuates randomly during CPR
quiz.why: A sudden, sustained rise in EtCO2 during CPR, without a change in compression quality, is a recognized sign that spontaneous circulation may have returned, prompting a pulse and rhythm check.

quiz.q: A ventilated ICU boarder's EtCO2 has been stable at 40 mmHg for hours, then drops abruptly to 15 mmHg. The ventilator is still cycling, and the tube position looks unchanged on exam. What should be considered first?
choices: A benign lab drawing error
Normal breath-to-breath variability
The patient has started breathing spontaneously
A sudden drop in pulmonary blood flow, such as a massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac arrest, or severe hypotension
quiz.why: With ventilation unchanged and no circuit problem, an abrupt EtCO2 drop points toward a circulatory catastrophe reducing blood flow to the lungs — this is treated as an emergency, not a lab artifact.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure is being taken with a cuff that is far too large for a very thin arm. What artifact should be anticipated?
choices: A falsely low reading
A falsely high reading
No meaningful change from the true value
Complete failure of the cuff to cycle
quiz.why: An oversized cuff underestimates blood pressure, producing a falsely low reading — the mirror-image error from an undersized cuff, which reads falsely high.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has an IV infusing in the right arm and a suspected fracture of the left arm. Where should the blood pressure cuff be placed?
choices: The right arm, over the running IV, since it is otherwise unused
Neither arm is ideal — use a properly sized thigh cuff or document the constraint and choose the least harmful option per protocol
The left arm over the suspected fracture, since it is closer to the heart
Skip blood pressure entirely until imaging is complete
quiz.why: A cuff over an infusing IV can cause infiltration and pain, and cuffing an injured limb can worsen injury or falsify the reading. When both arms are compromised, an alternate site like the thigh, chosen and documented, is the safer approach.

quiz.q: An ESI level 4 patient with a minor laceration has been stable in the waiting room. What is a typical vitals reassessment interval for this acuity level?
choices: Every 15 minutes
Every 30 minutes
Roughly every 1 to 4 hours, or with any change in condition
Continuous monitoring is required regardless of acuity
quiz.why: Lower-acuity patients (ESI 4-5) are reassessed on a much longer interval than critical patients, typically every 1 to 4 hours, with any new symptom prompting an earlier check.

quiz.q: A patient's heart rate is 140 and systolic blood pressure is 132. What does the shock index suggest?
choices: About 0.94 — within the normal range, so no concern
About 0.9 — right at the normal cutoff
About 1.9 — this indicates the patient is in profound decompensated shock
About 1.06 — concerning for compensated shock
quiz.why: 140 divided by 132 is about 1.06, above the 0.9 threshold, flagging possible compensated shock even though the blood pressure alone still looks reasonable.

quiz.q: Which of the following best demonstrates 'trend plus number plus observation' communication about a patient?
choices: "His heart rate climbed from 88 to 114 over the last hour, and he is now diaphoretic and less talkative."
"He looks worse than before."
"His heart rate is up."
"Something about him is bothering me."
quiz.why: Naming the specific trend, the actual numbers, and a physical observation gives a listener something concrete and actionable, unlike vague impressions.

quiz.q: A patient's urine output over the last two hours totals 60 mL, and he weighs 80 kg. Is this adequate?
choices: Yes, this is well above the minimum threshold
No, this is below the roughly 0.5 mL/kg/h threshold suggesting inadequate organ perfusion
It cannot be assessed without a creatinine level
Urine output is not a useful perfusion marker in adults
quiz.why: 0.5 mL/kg/h for an 80 kg patient over 2 hours would be 80 mL; 60 mL falls short of that threshold, suggesting reduced kidney perfusion and possible early shock.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure drifts down slightly over four rechecks while heart rate climbs, but every individual value remains inside the alarm limits the whole time. What does this scenario illustrate?
choices: That alarm limits alone are sufficient to catch deterioration
That this pattern is always benign and requires no comment
That deterioration can be missed by alarms because it shows as a trend across values, not a single out-of-range number
That the monitor is malfunctioning
quiz.why: A trend across otherwise 'in range' numbers is exactly the kind of deterioration that alarm thresholds are not designed to catch — comparing values over time is what reveals it.

quiz.q: A patient meets two SIRS criteria and has a suspected pneumonia. Does this alone confirm sepsis?
choices: Yes, meeting SIRS criteria is sufficient by itself to diagnose sepsis
No, SIRS criteria are only used for trauma patients
Yes, but only if the temperature criterion is one of the two met
No, SIRS criteria flag a systemic inflammatory response and prompt further evaluation, but sepsis requires evidence of infection with organ dysfunction
quiz.why: SIRS is a screening tool for systemic inflammation, not a sepsis diagnosis on its own. It prompts the workup that determines whether infection with organ dysfunction (sepsis) is actually present.

quiz.q: A patient meets a qSOFA score of 2. What does this specifically flag?
choices: An increased risk of mortality from suspected infection, prompting more thorough evaluation and escalation
A definite diagnosis of severe sepsis requiring immediate intubation
That the patient does not have an infection
That antibiotics can be safely delayed for several hours
quiz.why: A qSOFA of 2 or more identifies patients with suspected infection who are at meaningfully higher risk of poor outcomes, which is meant to trigger prompt further assessment and escalation, not a specific treatment by itself.

quiz.q: On the NEWS2 scoring system, a patient scores a 3 on a single parameter (for example, a very low respiratory rate) but a total score of only 4 overall. What does the NEWS2 approach say about this?
choices: The low total score means no escalation is needed
A single parameter scoring 3 triggers escalation on its own, the same as a higher aggregate total would
Only the aggregate total ever matters, regardless of any individual score
This combination is not addressed by NEWS2
quiz.why: NEWS2 is designed so that one severely abnormal parameter escalates care even if the total score looks moderate, because a single extreme value can represent real danger that averaging would hide.

quiz.q: Compressions are in progress on an adult and no advanced airway is placed yet. What is the correct ventilation approach?
choices: Continuous compressions with no interruption for ventilation at all
Deliver a breath every 2 seconds regardless of compressions
Pause compressions briefly every 30 compressions to deliver 2 breaths
Ventilate only if the patient begins to gasp
quiz.why: Without an advanced airway, CPR uses cycles of 30 compressions followed by a brief pause for 2 breaths, as opposed to the continuous asynchronous approach used once an advanced airway is in place.

quiz.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a shockable rhythm. Where are defibrillator pads typically placed?
choices: Both pads on the anterior chest directly over the sternum
Both pads on the patient's back
Pad placement does not matter as long as they touch skin
Anterolateral: one pad below the right clavicle, one at the left mid-axillary line, on dry bare skin
quiz.why: Standard anterolateral placement — one pad on the upper right chest, one at the left lower ribs/mid-axillary line — on dry, bare skin gives the current the best path through the heart.

quiz.q: During a code, the team leader calls for the first dose of epinephrine. What is the standard adult dose and the interval before the next dose?
choices: 1 mg, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes
0.5 mg, repeated every minute
1 mg, given only once total
10 mg, repeated every 10 minutes
quiz.why: Adult cardiac arrest epinephrine dosing is 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes throughout the resuscitation, a detail every team member should be able to anticipate and call out.

quiz.q: A patient with restraints in place for agitation has not had a documented circulation check in over an hour, though policy calls for checks roughly every 15 minutes. What is the concern?
choices: No real concern, since the patient appears comfortable
A missed safety check that could allow nerve or vascular injury to go undetected
This interval is actually more frequent than required
Only skin color needs to be checked, not circulation
quiz.why: Restraints can compromise circulation or cause nerve injury if left unchecked. Regular, timely checks are a patient safety requirement, not an optional courtesy.

quiz.q: A ventilator's low-pressure alarm sounds. What is the correct technician action?
choices: Increase the pressure limit on the ventilator to stop the alarm
Silence the alarm and continue routine tasks
Look at the patient for signs of disconnection or leak, and immediately notify respiratory therapy and the nurse
Adjust the tidal volume setting
quiz.why: Technicians never adjust ventilator settings. A low-pressure alarm often signals a disconnection or leak — the correct response is to assess the patient and circuit visually and get respiratory therapy involved immediately.

quiz.q: A patient one hour after thrombolytic administration for stroke has a stable exam and blood pressure within target. What should still happen during this window?
choices: Checks can be spaced out to once per hour since things look stable
Monitoring can stop once the infusion is complete
Only blood pressure needs to be checked, not neuro status
Neuro checks and blood pressure continue every 15 minutes for the full 2-hour high-risk window regardless of current stability
quiz.why: The post-thrombolytic bleeding risk persists through the defined monitoring window even if the patient looks fine at any given moment, so the frequent check schedule is maintained regardless of apparent stability.

quiz.q: A high heart-rate alarm sounds and the bedside trace shows a jagged, unrecognizable waveform while the patient is calmly talking on the phone. Applying the alarm algorithm, what is this most consistent with?
choices: Motion or lead artifact, since the waveform doesn't match a clean rhythm and the patient looks well
A genuine, dangerous tachyarrhythmia requiring immediate defibrillation
A normal sinus rhythm
Equipment that must be replaced before further use
quiz.why: The first algorithm question — does the waveform match the number — fails here: a jagged, unreadable trace with a comfortable, talking patient points to artifact rather than a true dangerous rhythm.

quiz.q: An alarm indicates a very low respiratory rate on a patient who is actually snoring loudly and appears to be in a deep, difficult-to-rouse sleep after opioid administration. What should the technician do?
choices: Assume it is impedance artifact from the snoring and ignore it
Treat this as a possible real event — assess responsiveness and breathing directly rather than assuming artifact
Silence it since the patient appears to be resting comfortably
Wait until the next scheduled round to check
quiz.why: Snoring with a low respiratory rate after opioids is a red flag for hypoventilation, not a reassuring sign to be waved off as artifact — this patient needs to be assessed directly and immediately.

quiz.q: A five-lead ECG cable becomes disconnected at the chest lead (brown wire) during ambulation. What is the most likely effect on the monitor?
choices: No change at all to any displayed parameter
Complete shutdown of the monitor
Loss of the chest lead view (commonly V1) while limb leads may still display, possibly triggering a lead-off alarm
The SpO2 will also stop reading
quiz.why: Each electrode contributes to specific derived leads; losing the chest (V1) lead affects that view and commonly triggers a lead-off alarm, while the limb leads can remain functional.

quiz.q: A patient's ECG trace has been noisy since admission. The technician notes the electrodes have not been changed in three days. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Increase the gain setting to compensate for the noise
Leave them in place since changing electrodes rarely helps
Switch to a different monitor entirely
Replace the electrodes and re-prep the skin, since electrodes are typically changed roughly every 24 hours
quiz.why: Electrode gel dries out and adhesion weakens over time; routine replacement (about every 24 hours, and after defibrillation) along with proper skin prep resolves most persistent noisy-trace problems.

quiz.q: A diaphoretic patient's telemetry keeps losing signal intermittently, and the electrodes look intact and properly placed. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Dry the skin thoroughly, remove oils, and consider a skin-prep or adhesive product before reapplying electrodes
Increase the alarm volume so it is heard sooner
Move the patient to a different room
Switch from a 5-lead to a 3-lead system, which never has this problem
quiz.why: Moisture and skin oils are the most common causes of poor electrode adhesion and signal loss in diaphoretic patients; drying and prepping the skin before reapplying electrodes addresses the root cause.

quiz.q: A capnogram shows normal-appearing waveforms but a phase 3 plateau that slopes noticeably upward instead of staying flat. What condition does this pattern suggest?
choices: Normal ventilation with no abnormality
Obstructive airway disease, such as bronchospasm, causing uneven emptying of the lungs
Esophageal placement of the airway
Rebreathing of exhaled gas
quiz.why: An upsloping (rather than flat) plateau reflects uneven, delayed alveolar emptying typical of obstructive processes like bronchospasm, distinct from the classic shark-fin picture but related to the same mechanism.

quiz.q: A sedated patient's capnography shows a normal waveform shape but a slowly rising EtCO2 alongside a falling respiratory rate over several minutes. What should this trend prompt?
choices: No action, since the waveform shape itself is normal
Immediate discontinuation of capnography monitoring
Concern for opioid-related hypoventilation, prompting stimulation and provider notification
Assumption of a sensor drift requiring recalibration only
quiz.why: A rising EtCO2 with a falling respiratory rate, even with a normal-shaped waveform, is the classic early pattern of opioid-induced hypoventilation and calls for direct intervention, not reassurance from the waveform shape alone.

quiz.q: A patient in early septic shock is breathing rapidly to compensate for a developing metabolic acidosis. What would you expect to see on capnography, and why?
choices: A high EtCO2, because rapid breathing increases CO2 production
No change in EtCO2, since capnography does not reflect metabolic status
An erratic, unreadable waveform with no clinical meaning
A low EtCO2, because the patient is hyperventilating to blow off CO2 and partially compensate for the acidosis
quiz.why: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis works by increasing minute ventilation to blow off CO2, which lowers EtCO2 — a low value here reflects appropriate compensation for the underlying metabolic problem, not a ventilation failure.

quiz.q: A 90 kg patient in septic shock requires the standard hour-1 crystalloid bolus. What volume should be targeted, and what access is needed?
choices: 2700 mL through large-bore access, delivered under pressure rather than by gravity
900 mL through a small-bore peripheral IV
5400 mL over the first hour regardless of clinical response
1800 mL is the fixed dose regardless of weight
quiz.why: 30 mL/kg for a 90 kg patient is 2700 mL; delivering that volume promptly requires large-bore IV access and a pressure bag or rapid infuser rather than gravity flow.

quiz.q: Antibiotics were given promptly, but blood cultures were drawn 45 minutes after the antibiotics infused, not before. What is the clinical consequence?
choices: None; timing of cultures relative to antibiotics does not matter
Culture sensitivity may be reduced, since antibiotics can suppress organism growth, making it harder to identify the causative pathogen
The antibiotics themselves become less effective
The lactate result becomes invalid
quiz.why: Drawing cultures after antibiotics have started reduces the chance of growing the causative organism, which can hamper de-escalation and targeted therapy later — this is why cultures are drawn first whenever feasible.

quiz.q: A patient's initial lactate on arrival was 3.2 mmol/L. Two hours later, after fluids and antibiotics, it is 1.8 mmol/L. What does this trend suggest?
choices: Worsening sepsis requiring escalation of care
A lab error that should be repeated immediately
Lactate clearance, a favorable sign that treatment is improving tissue perfusion
No clinical significance since lactate values fluctuate randomly
quiz.why: A falling lactate after fluids and antibiotics reflects improving tissue perfusion and is one of the key reassessment markers used to judge whether sepsis treatment is working.

quiz.q: A patient is E4 V5 M6 on initial assessment. What is the total GCS, and what does each letter represent?
choices: 12 total; eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
15 total; energy, vitals, and mentation
10 total; eye opening, vocalization, and mobility
15 total; eye opening, verbal response, and motor response
quiz.why: GCS sums Eye (1-4), Verbal (1-5), and Motor (1-6) scores; 4+5+6 equals the maximum possible total of 15, representing a fully alert, oriented patient with normal motor response.

quiz.q: A patient's left pupil has been consistently 4mm and sluggish for the past day due to a known old eye injury, while the right pupil is 3mm and brisk. A new nurse flags this as an urgent finding. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: If this asymmetry is a documented chronic baseline, it is not a new finding — comparing to the patient's own prior exams matters more than an isolated snapshot
This is always urgent regardless of history
Pupil findings are never clinically significant
Only pupil reactivity matters, never size
quiz.why: A pupil finding must be compared against the patient's own baseline. A longstanding, documented asymmetry is very different from a new change, which is why trending each patient's exam over time matters more than any single reading.

quiz.q: A patient scores 0-42 on the NIHSS at two different times: 6 on arrival and 11 two hours later. What does this change most likely represent?
choices: Improvement in neurological status
Worsening neurological deficit, which should be reported and may prompt urgent reimaging
A scoring error, since NIHSS rarely changes over short periods
No clinical significance since both scores are 'mild'
quiz.why: A rising NIHSS score reflects an increasing neurological deficit and is treated as a real, reportable change — trending the score matters more than any single value in isolation.

quiz.q: A patient with a GI bleed has a heart rate rising from 92 to 118 over 90 minutes while blood pressure stays technically within the alarm limits the entire time. What does the pattern most likely represent?
choices: Reassuring stability since the pressure never alarmed
A benign anxiety response with no clinical significance
Compensated shock progressing, evidenced by a worsening trend even though no single value has crossed an alarm threshold
An equipment malfunction requiring recalibration
quiz.why: The trend itself — a steadily climbing heart rate — is the warning, independent of whether any single blood pressure value has yet crossed an alarm limit. Watching trends catches this before alarms would.

quiz.q: An elderly patient who was pleasant and conversational all morning suddenly becomes withdrawn and cannot answer a simple orientation question in the afternoon. Vital signs are all within normal limits. What should this prompt?
choices: No action, since vitals are normal
Assuming this is simply fatigue from a long day
Waiting until the next scheduled round to mention it
Treating the new confusion itself as a vital sign, prompting reassessment and notification even though the monitor shows nothing abnormal
quiz.why: New confusion can be an early sign of deterioration — infection, hypoperfusion, or another process — well before vital signs change, which is why mental status is treated as its own vital sign requiring the same urgency as an abnormal number.

quiz.q: A patient with known COPD has an SpO2 of 89% that has been stable and documented as his baseline. On a different shift, a new tech becomes alarmed at this number and considers escalating urgently. What is the correct framing?
choices: A documented, stable baseline changes the meaning of a number — the same reading in a different patient without that history would be far more concerning
This is always an emergency regardless of documented baseline
SpO2 numbers never require any clinical context
The number should be reported as critical regardless of history
quiz.why: Interpreting any single number requires knowing the individual patient's baseline and trend. The same value can be reassuring in one patient and alarming in another, which is why context and trend matter more than a raw threshold.

quiz.q: A 10-year-old presents after a fall. What is the estimated lower limit of normal systolic blood pressure using the standard pediatric formula?
choices: 70 mmHg
90 mmHg
80 mmHg
100 mmHg
quiz.why: 70 plus (2 times 10) equals 90 mmHg, the estimated lower limit of normal systolic pressure for a 10-year-old under the standard rule.

quiz.q: A toddler is crying and thrashing during vital sign measurement, producing a heart rate of 190 and an erratic SpO2 reading. What is the best approach?
choices: Chart the numbers exactly as displayed and treat them as accurate
Restrain the child firmly to obtain an accurate reading
Allow the child to calm on a caregiver's lap and reassess once settled, since an upset child produces artifact-prone readings
Assume the equipment is broken and switch monitors
quiz.why: An agitated child generates unreliable vitals from motion and crying. Allowing the child to settle, often on a parent's lap, produces far more trustworthy numbers than forcing a reading during distress.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with a febrile illness has flaring nostrils, visible head bobbing with each breath, and grunting on exhalation. What do these findings together indicate?
choices: Mild, self-limited illness needing no urgent evaluation
Normal findings for a febrile, anxious child
A sign of dehydration only, unrelated to breathing effort
Signs of severe respiratory distress requiring prompt evaluation
quiz.why: Grunting, head bobbing, and nasal flaring are recognized markers of severe pediatric respiratory distress and should prompt urgent assessment rather than being dismissed as typical fussiness.

quiz.q: During procedural sedation, a patient's RASS is scored as +2 (frequent, non-purposeful movement, agitated). What does this suggest about the current sedation level?
choices: The patient is under-sedated relative to the usual 0 to -2 target range and may need dose adjustment
The patient is appropriately sedated for most ED procedures
The patient is over-sedated and at risk of apnea
RASS is not used to guide sedation level, only recovery
quiz.why: A RASS of +2 is agitated, above the typical ED sedation target of 0 to -2, indicating the patient is not adequately sedated for the procedure and may need reassessment of dosing.

quiz.q: A patient's Aldrete score is calculated at 7 because his blood pressure remains more than 20 mmHg below his pre-procedure baseline, though every other category is fully scored. What does this mean for discharge readiness?
choices: He can be discharged since most categories scored well
He does not yet meet the usual discharge threshold of 9 or more and needs further monitoring of that specific parameter
Aldrete does not need to reach any specific number before discharge
The score should simply be rounded up to 9
quiz.why: Discharge after procedural sedation typically requires an Aldrete score of 9 or higher; a persistently low circulation score, even with everything else normal, means the patient has not yet met criteria.

quiz.q: A patient receiving procedural sedation requires a jaw thrust to maintain airway patency partway through the procedure. What is the significance of documenting this?
choices: It is a routine, insignificant part of any sedation and does not need separate documentation
It only needs to be mentioned if the patient later has complications
It represents an airway intervention that reflects a level of sedation depth requiring active management, and its timing matters for the record
Jaw thrusts are never needed during procedural sedation
quiz.why: Any airway intervention during sedation, including a jaw thrust, signals that the patient reached a depth of sedation requiring active airway support, which is important to document with its exact time for the clinical record.

quiz.q: A technician calling a rapid response says, "Room 12, 58-year-old, I think something might be going on, could someone check when they're free?" What is wrong with this call?
choices: Nothing; this communicates the urgency clearly
It is too long and should be shortened further
The room number should come last, not first
It lacks specific numbers, a clear trend, and a direct, immediate request for someone at the bedside
quiz.why: An effective rapid response call states specific abnormal numbers and a trend, then makes a direct, immediate ask — vague language and soft phrasing let the request get deprioritized.

quiz.q: While waiting for a rapid response team to arrive, what should the calling technician have ready at the bedside?
choices: A full set of vitals, the monitor, oxygen and suction available, and the doorway cleared for access
Nothing extra; simply wait by the door
The patient's insurance and billing information
A printed copy of the chart only
quiz.why: Preparing oxygen, suction, monitoring, and a clear path into the room means the arriving team can act immediately rather than losing time gathering basic equipment on arrival.

quiz.q: During shift handoff of a monitored patient, the outgoing tech mentions vitals, alarm limits, and pending labs, but omits that the SpO2 probe reads unreliably on this particular patient's fingers. Why does this omission matter?
choices: It doesn't matter, since the incoming tech will discover it on their own
The incoming tech may trust a falsely reassuring or falsely alarming number without knowing to double-check it by another method
SpO2 reliability issues are always obvious from the waveform alone
This detail belongs in the chart, not in verbal handoff
quiz.why: A known unreliable reading is exactly the kind of practical knowledge that doesn't show up automatically on the screen — omitting it risks the next caregiver either missing a real problem or chasing a false one.

quiz.q: A monitored patient must be transported to the OR, and the assigned escort has never operated the transport monitor being used. What is the correct action before leaving the unit?
choices: Proceed anyway since transport time is short
Leave the monitor behind since it is unfamiliar equipment
Ensure the escort is familiar with the transport monitor and its alarms before departure, or assign someone who is
Transport without any monitor and reconnect on arrival
quiz.why: A transport monitor is only useful if the escort can actually interpret and respond to it. Ensuring competence with the equipment before departure is part of the safety requirement, not an afterthought.
